extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, public opinion, and democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Critical analysis of institutional features and practical criteria for stable representative government, especially comparing constitutional checks, patronage, and guild-socialist proposals. Focuses on what makes governance workable (information, unit size, coercion, representation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances as remedy for public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition." (Federalist No. 51) — the constitutional system balances special interests so men can be governed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine was intended to deadlock local and class interests to prevent obstruction of government, and to 'enable the government to control the governed' while obliging it 'to control itself.' Not intended to produce perpetual deadlock but to neutralize narrow local opinion as a substitute for coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional design to limit popular rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution was "a candid attempt to limit the sphere of popular rule; the only democratic organ it was intended the government should possess was the House, based on a suffrage highly limited by property qualifications."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional choices (electoral college, Senate, veto, judicial interpretation) reflect an explicit intent to check popular impulses; evaluation should consider what parts of a constitution were meant to restrict popular rule versus enable it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation and political myth as sustaining institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Jefferson taught Americans to regard the Constitution as an instrument of democracy; public perception (the 'fiction' of a democratic Constitution) reshaped practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How people read and talk about institutions can effectively rewrite their spirit; the legitimacy and endurance of constitutional arrangements depend on collective stereotypes and accepted narratives as much as on formal structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage as a tool for national cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Patronage and rotation in office created a new governing class and 'we often fail to realize how much of the stability of our government we owe to patronage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patronage can wean local leaders toward national cooperation by attaching incentives; reforms that remove patronage must account for its stabilizing effects and unintended creation of professional politicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale mismatch of democratic images and political reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the township model (rotation, short terms) to a large national polity produces different, often adverse, results (creation of professional politicians, sophisticated electioneering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reforms by checking whether the ideal's environmental assumptions (small, familiar communities) hold at larger scales; the same normative principle can have opposite practical effects when scaled up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of systematic information and analysis for legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: A congress of representatives is 'essentially a group of blind men in a vast, unknown world' — legislators need controlled reporting and objective analysis, not merely exchanged local impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective national lawmaking requires instruments (bureaus, data, expert analysis) that provide standardized, comparable information; absence of such instruments leads to superficial deliberation and dependence on insiders or partisan force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem of one-sided executive information
rubrics_metrics.description: The President has access to a vast collection of bureaus and agents and can deliver messages based on what he chooses to tell Congress; this creates a 'wholly one-sided and tricky relationship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While administrative apparatus can inform policy, reliance on executive reports without checks creates informational bias; institutional design should mitigate censoring or selective disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional investigation as poor substitute for regular information
rubrics_metrics.description: When Congress lacks legitimate informational resources it resorts to investigations that yield little and are sensational ('wild and feverish man-hunt').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate legislative capacity by the quality and availability of routine, impartial information rather than episodic investigations; good governance needs institutionalized data flows, not ad hoc inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localism and logrolling as outcomes of informational poverty
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislatures without effective analysis oscillate between 'blind regularity, tempered by occasional insurgency, and logrolling' where local items are traded and aggregated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of national-scale information favors parceling laws into local benefits (pork) and logrolling; assessments should track whether deliberation produces coherent national policy or merely bundles local favors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of common consciousness determines reliance on force or patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Either governance depends on force (autocracy) or on a developed system of information and self-consciousness; where the voluntary system is underdeveloped, patronage and privilege substitute for common consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating prospects for large-scale cooperation (federal unions, leagues, industrial governance), measure how much material (information, shared understanding) for a common consciousness exists; low common consciousness implies greater reliance on coercion or patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coercive powers implicitly required in non-coercive schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: In Guild Socialism, the Commune is given many functions (fixing prices, allocating resources, levying taxes, declaring war, running the police) — functions that amount to coercive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any plan aiming to be 'non-coercive' must be examined for the actual powers it allocates; enumerated administrative powers are indicators of de facto sovereignty and coercion even when theoretical language denies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledging force in transitions to new regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Cole 'is too honest to shirk the element of force required to make the transition' to guild society; trade unions' direct action and potential civil war are admitted possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of institutional change must account for the coercive element in transitions; utopian schemes that ignore how they come into being are incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factory/shop as the natural unit for industrial democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The factory (or shop, mine, dock, station) is 'the natural and fundamental unit of industrial democracy' — an environment small enough for direct, personal self-government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic units should be small enough that members can know matters 'at a single view'; when designing representative structures, verify that base units are actually familiar environments to participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of shop democracy on external relations
rubrics_metrics.description: While the shop can self-govern 'internal affairs' that are directly knowable, its opinions about plant-wide, industry-wide, or national matters transcend direct experience and are thus unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-government works for proximate matters but cannot supply competent judgments on translocal issues without instruments for broader information, education, or coordinated representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional representation does not eliminate the knowledge problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Guildsmen propose representatives who act for 'some particular function' rather than territorial groups; yet representatives must still judge proposals on issues beyond their direct shop experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional representation assumes workers know functional interests by experience, but where issues transcend immediate function, delegates still need broader knowledge and deliberative instruments; otherwise decisions risk being parochial, logrolled, or chaotic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of a common or informed will requires education/propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: The public opinions of a shop about its duties in the industry 'are matters of education or propaganda, not the automatic product of shop-consciousness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For representative democracy (territorial or functional) to produce informed choices on complex external affairs, active processes of education, communication, and deliberate formation of opinion are necessary; spontaneous shop views are insufficient.
